name: Data-Driven Farm Management with Mobile Apps
objectives: Given a list of what your farm needs to track, compare farm management apps or a shared spreadsheet against a feature checklist and choose one, scoring at least two options and writing the reason for your choice

chapters.name: Chapter 1: Setting up your farm system

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Choosing a farm app or a shared spreadsheet
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose a farm management app or a shared spreadsheet by scoring it against a feature checklist.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of what your farm needs to track, you will compare farm management apps or a shared spreadsheet against a feature checklist and choose one, scoring at least two options and writing the reason for your choice.
A farm management app keeps your fields, animals, work, stock and money in one place on your phone. Many exist, and they change often, so this course does not recommend one. A free shared spreadsheet (Google Sheets or Microsoft Excel) can do the same job if you set it up well. What matters is that you and your workers actually use it every day.
Start with what you need to track, then score each option. Features to look for: works offline and syncs later (many farms have weak network); fields and animal groups as separate records; a simple way to log activities and inputs; stock levels that go down when inputs are used; worker and payment records; photos; several users with different access (a worker can enter data but not see payroll); export to a spreadsheet so your data is never locked in; your language; and a clear price and privacy policy.
Be careful with apps that are free because they sell your data, that need a fast connection, or that you cannot leave with your data. Ask other farmers in your area what they use, try any app for two weeks with real entries, and check the price after the free trial before you put all your records in it.
Step by step:
- List what you must track: fields, animals, work, workers, stock, sales.
- Pick two or three options, including a free shared spreadsheet.
- Score each one against the checklist: offline, users and access, stock, workers, photos, export, language, price, privacy.
- Try the best one for two weeks with real entries.
- Write down your choice and why.
Words to know:
- Farm management app: a phone or web program for recording and organising a farm's fields, animals, work, stock and money.
- Sync: when an app sends the data saved on the phone to the internet once there is network.
- Export: saving your data out of an app, for example as a spreadsheet file.
Try it now: Write the list of what your farm must track. Make a scoring table with the checklist features down the side and two or three options across the top (one can be a free shared spreadsheet). Score each one and write your choice and your reason.
You can now judge any farm app or spreadsheet by its features and choose one with a clear reason.

check.q: Your farm in Kakamega often has no network. Which feature matters most?
check.why: If the app cannot save entries without network, workers will stop using it.

check.q: Why check that an app can export your data?
options: So your records are never locked inside one app
Because the law requires every farmer to export
check.why: Export lets you move your records to a spreadsheet or another app at any time.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Setting up fields, animals, activities and input stock
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Set up a farm register with fixed names, units and an input stock list.
This lesson builds toward: Using the tool you chose, you will set up a farm register of fields, animals, activities and input stock with fixed names and units, so every entry can be added up by field, animal group or input.
A register is the backbone of the system. Give every field a fixed short name and size (for example "F1 Tomato 0.5 acre"), and every animal group or pond a name and count ("Layers House A, 500 birds", "Goats 24", "Pond 2 tilapia"). Use the same names in every record so you can add up cost and output by field or group.
Then make an activity log: date, field or group, activity (planting, weeding, spraying, feeding, vaccinating by the vet, harvesting, selling), quantity, unit, cost, who did it and a photo if useful. Fix the units: kilograms, litres, bags of 50 kg, crates, trays of 30 eggs. Mixed units make totals wrong.
Add an input stock list: each input with its unit, stock in, stock used and stock left. When a worker records "2 bags NPK used on F1", the stock left should go down by two. Count the store against the list every week. If the count and the record do not match, you have found a leak, a recording mistake or theft, and you can ask why the same week.
Step by step:
- Name every field with size, and every animal group, pond or house with its count.
- Fix units for each item: kg, litres, 50 kg bags, crates, trays.
- Make the activity log: date, field or group, activity, quantity, unit, cost, who, photo.
- Make the stock list: input, unit, in, used, left.
- Count the store weekly and compare with the list.
Words to know:
- Register: the master list of your fields, animal groups and inputs that every record refers to.
- Unit: what you measure in, such as kilograms, litres or 50 kg bags.
- Stock count: physically counting what is in the store and comparing it with the records.
Try it now: In your chosen tool, create the register for your farm: every field or animal group with its size or count, an activity log with at least five real entries from this week, and a stock list for at least four inputs. Then count one input in your store and compare it with the list.
You can now set up a farm register that adds up by field, animal group and input, and check your stock against it.

check.q: One worker writes "2 bags" and another writes "100 kg" for the same fertilizer. What is the fix?
options: Ignore it; the total will be close enough
Fix one unit for that input and use it every time
check.why: Fixed units let you add up records correctly.

check.q: The stock list says 6 bags of layers mash, but the store has 4. What do you do?
options: Wait until the end of the season
Buy 2 more bags and say nothing
Ask this week why they differ: recording mistake, leak or theft
check.why: A weekly count catches gaps while they are small and easy to explain.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Tracking labour and paying workers by mobile money
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Record each worker's days and tasks and pay them by mobile money with a matching record.
This lesson builds toward: Given a week of work by casual and permanent workers, you will record each worker's days and tasks and pay them by mobile money with a matching record, so every payment has a date, worker, task, amount and transaction code.
Labour is often the biggest cost on a growing farm and the least recorded. Keep a worker list (name, phone number for mobile money, daily or monthly rate, start date) and a daily attendance and task log: date, worker, field or group, task, days or hours. A supervisor can send it as a WhatsApp photo of the attendance sheet or fill a shared form every evening.
Pay by mobile money where you can: M-Pesa in Kenya, MTN MoMo in Ghana, Orange Money or Wave in Senegal and Côte d'Ivoire, or a bank or mobile money transfer in Nigeria. Every payment then has a transaction code. Copy the date, worker, amount and transaction code into your payment record, next to the days worked. At the end of the week the days times the rate should equal what you paid. Example only: 6 days x KES 500 = KES 3,000, or 5 days x NGN 4,000 = NGN 20,000.
Pay fairly and on time, and check the legal minimum wage and labour rules with your country's ministry of labour. Do not let children do hazardous farm work such as spraying, handling chemicals or using machines. Tell workers what you record and why, and confirm each payment with them, so the record protects both sides.
Step by step:
- Keep a worker list: name, mobile money number, rate, start date.
- Log attendance and tasks every day.
- Pay by mobile money and copy the transaction code into the payment record.
- Each week check: days x rate = amount paid.
- Confirm each payment with the worker.
Words to know:
- Casual worker: a worker paid by the day or task, not on a monthly contract.
- Transaction code: the unique code in the mobile money message that proves a payment happened.
- Payroll: the record of who is paid how much and when.
Official sources:
- FAO: Child labour in agriculture
Try it now: Make a worker list and a one-week attendance and task log for your farm (real or example). Fill a payment record with date, worker, days, rate, amount and a transaction code column, and check that days times rate equals the amount for every worker.
You can now track who worked, on what and for how long, and pay workers by mobile money with a record that matches.

options: "12 May, Juma, 6 days weeding F2, KES 3,000 (example), code QX7..."
check.why: It has the date, worker, task, days, amount and transaction code.

check.q: A worker says she worked 6 days; the log shows 5. What helps most?
options: The daily attendance log and a talk with her and the supervisor
Taking the higher number without asking
check.why: A daily log gives both sides a record to check together.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Managing with data, near or far

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Protecting farm and worker data
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Decide what data to collect, who can see it and how to protect it.
This lesson builds toward: When you collect data about your farm and your workers, you will decide what to collect, who can see it and how to protect it, collecting only what you need and sharing no PINs, passwords or ID numbers.
Your system now holds valuable and private information: workers' names and phone numbers, pay, your sales and your stock. Kenya (Office of the Data Protection Commissioner), Nigeria (Nigeria Data Protection Commission) and Ghana (Data Protection Commission) have data protection laws and regulators, and so do many other African countries. Larger farms and businesses may have to register; check your regulator's website.
Collect only what you need. You need a worker's name, mobile money number, days and pay. You do not need their ID number in a shared sheet or a photo of their ID in a WhatsApp group. Tell workers what you keep and why. Never put mobile money PINs, passwords or ID numbers in the sheet, the app or an AI tool.
Set access by role: workers enter activities; the manager sees stock and attendance; only you (and your accountant) see pay and sales. Use a phone lock and two-step sign-in, remove people who leave the farm the same day, and keep a backup. If you share data with a buyer, lender or project, share only what they need and ask how they will use it.
Step by step:
- List the data you hold and cross out what you do not need.
- Tell workers what you record and why.
- Set access by role: worker, manager, owner.
- Lock phones, turn on two-step sign-in, keep a backup.
- Remove access for anyone who leaves, the same day.
Words to know:
- Personal data: information about a person, such as a name, phone number or pay.
- Access: who can see or change which data.
- Two-step sign-in: a second check, such as a code sent to your phone, when you sign in.
Official sources:
- Office of the Data Protection Commissioner (Kenya)
- Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC)
- Data Protection Commission, Ghana (Data Protection Act, 2012, Act 843)
Try it now: List every kind of data in your farm system. Cross out what you do not need. Write an access table: for each role (worker, manager, owner, accountant), what they can see and what they can enter.
You can now collect only the data your farm needs and control who can see it.

check.q: Which should NOT go in the shared farm sheet?
check.why: PINs are secret; nobody else should ever hold them.

check.q: Your manager leaves the farm. When do you remove his access to the farm sheet and app?
options: At the end of the season
check.why: Removing access the same day protects your data and your workers' data.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Managing the farm from a distance
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a daily reporting routine that you can verify.
This lesson builds toward: When a manager or family member runs the farm while you are away, you will write a daily reporting routine with photo and WhatsApp reports, a weekly check-in and spot checks, saying what to report, by when, and how you will verify it.
Many owners run farms from town through a manager or a relative. It works when the reporting is routine, not when you call randomly and ask "How is everything?". Agree a daily WhatsApp report by a fixed time, for example 6 pm: what was done in each field or house, numbers (eggs collected, birds dead, feed used, litres of milk, crates sold, workers present), problems, and three photos of the same places each day (the crop, the animals, the store).
Hold a short weekly check-in by phone or video at a fixed time: go through the week's numbers, the stock count and next week's plan. Decide together and write the decisions in the group. A good manager should also be paid and trusted to make small decisions without you.
Trust, but verify. Compare reports with things that are hard to fake: mobile money statements, buyer receipts, the weekly stock count and photos with the date and location. Visit without long notice now and then, and sometimes ask a trusted neighbour, vet or extension officer for a second view. When a number looks wrong, ask calmly and early. Most gaps are mistakes, and checking regularly keeps honest people honest.
Step by step:
- Agree the daily report: time, numbers, problems, three fixed photos.
- Set a weekly check-in at a fixed time.
- Write decisions in the group.
- Verify with statements, receipts, stock counts and dated photos.
- Visit sometimes without long notice; ask early and calmly about odd numbers.
Words to know:
- Absentee owner: a farm owner who lives away and runs the farm through someone else.
- Verify: check that a report is true using a second source.
- Check-in: a short, regular meeting to review numbers and plans.
Try it now: Write the daily report template your manager will send (the numbers, the problems line and the three photo spots). Then list three ways you will verify the reports, and the day and time of your weekly check-in.
You can now set up a daily report and weekly check-in with a manager and verify what they tell you.

check.q: Which daily report is most useful from a poultry manager?
options: A voice note at any time of day
"6 pm: 412 eggs, 2 birds dead, 3 bags feed used, 4 workers, photos of House A, birds and store"
check.why: Fixed numbers and photos at a fixed time can be compared day to day.

check.q: Which is the best way to verify reported egg sales?
options: Compare them with mobile money statements and buyer receipts
Ask the manager if he is sure
Count the eggs on the WhatsApp photo
Trust it because he is family
check.why: Payments and receipts are a second source that is hard to fake.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Your weekly dashboard: five numbers to watch
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Build a weekly dashboard of five numbers, each with a normal range and an action.
This lesson builds toward: Using your farm register, you will build a weekly dashboard of five numbers and the action each one triggers, updated every week from records, not from memory. When a manager or family member runs the farm while you are away, you will write a daily reporting routine with photo and WhatsApp reports, a weekly check-in and spot checks, saying what to report, by when, and how you will verify it.
A dashboard is a short page of the few numbers that tell you whether the farm is on track. Five is enough to read in two minutes every week. Choose numbers that come straight from your register, so nobody has to remember them.
Good choices for most farms: (1) cash in and cash out this week; (2) output, such as kg harvested, eggs per day, litres of milk or fish growth; (3) losses, such as dead birds, sick animals or rejected crates; (4) input stock left versus what the next two weeks need; (5) labour days or cost per field or group. A layer farm in Ghana might watch eggs per day, dead birds, feed used, cash from egg sales and feed stock. A tomato farmer in Senegal might watch crates harvested, rejected crates, labour days, cash from sales in XOF and pesticide and fertilizer stock.
For each number write a normal range and an action. Example: "Dead birds above 3 a day: call the vet the same day." "Feed stock below 10 days: order feed." Put the five numbers in a small table with one column per week, so you see the trend. Review it in the weekly check-in, and change a number if it never leads to a decision.
Step by step:
- Pick five numbers that come from your register.
- Write a normal range or target for each.
- Write the action if a number is outside the range.
- Make a table with one column per week.
- Review it in the weekly check-in and act.
Words to know:
- Dashboard: a short summary of the key numbers that show how the farm is doing.
- Trend: the direction a number moves over several weeks.
- Normal range: the values you expect when things are going well.
Try it now: Final task: build your weekly farm dashboard with five numbers, each with its source in your register, a normal range and the action you take if it is off, and fill in at least two weeks. Then write your one-page reporting routine: the daily report, the weekly check-in, how you verify, and who sees which data.
You can now run your farm with a weekly five-number dashboard and a reporting routine you can check.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Five useful numbers Fewer than five numbers, or numbers that lead to no decision. Five numbers covering cash, output, losses, stock and labour, each with a normal range and an action. At least two weeks filled in, and one decision already taken because of a number. Numbers come from records Numbers are guessed or remembered. Each number names its source in the register (activity log, stock list, payment record). The register uses fixed names and units, and the stock count matches the list. Labour and pay recorded Labour is missing or paid with no record. Labour days come from the attendance log and payments have transaction codes. Days x rate is checked against payments every week. Reporting routine No fixed report, or only "call when needed". Daily report content and time, weekly check-in, and at least two ways to verify are written. Includes unannounced visits or a trusted second view, and how odd numbers are raised. Data protected PINs, ID numbers or pay are visible to everyone. Only needed data is collected, and access is set by role. Includes backup, two-step sign-in and removing leavers the same day. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Why should dashboard numbers come straight from the register?
options: So nobody has to remember or guess them
check.why: Numbers from records are reliable; numbers from memory are not.

check.q: Your dashboard says "feed stock below 10 days: order feed". Stock is 6 days. What now?
options: Remove that number from the dashboard
Ask the workers to feed less
check.why: Each number has an action; when it is outside the range, you act.
